t: Guess the Number Using Bitwise Questions I
o: We must recover a hidden number n < 2^30 using only commonSetBits(num), which returns popcount(n & num). Since n has at most 30 bits, asking about each bit individually is natural: commonSetBits(1 << i) returns 1 if bit i of n is set (the AND has at most that single bit) and 0 otherwise. Example: n = 33 = 101111... no, 33 = 100001₂, so queries at bits 0 and 5 return 1 and all others return 0, reconstructing 33. Any strategy needs at least ~log2 information, and 30 queries is well within interactive limits.
k: With num = 2^i, commonSetBits returns exactly bit i of n, since n & num has at most one set bit.
30 queries suffice; adaptivity cannot beat one query per unknown bit here.
A divide-and-conquer on bit ranges reduces queries when n is sparse.

a.i: Query each of the 30 bit positions independently and OR the results together. Each answer directly reveals one bit of n.
s: If the result is nonzero, set bit i of the answer.
a.t: O(30) API calls, O(1) work per call.

a.n: Approach 2: Divide and conquer on bit ranges
a.i: First learn the total popcount with one query on the full mask. Then recursively split a bit range with c known set bits: query the mask of the lower half to learn how many of the c bits lie there, and recurse into both halves. Bits in empty ranges are skipped, so sparse n uses fewer queries.
s: recurse(lo, hi, cnt): if cnt == 0 stop; if the range is one bit, set it.
Otherwise query the lower-half mask, split cnt, and recurse into both halves.
a.t: At most 1 + 2·(number of branching nodes) ≤ 59 queries; often far fewer for sparse n.

w: The per-bit scan is the safest default: minimal code and provably 30 queries. The divide-and-conquer shines when the interviewer asks to minimize queries for sparse numbers. Pitfall: querying num outside [0, 2^30) makes results unreliable, and forgetting that the API returns a count, not a boolean (though with single-bit masks it is 0/1). Follow-up: minimize worst-case queries (information-theoretic bound ≈ ⌈30·log(2)/log(31)⌉ via group testing), or solve the variant where the API returns n AND num itself.
